props.title: Dinner with Friends

sections.content: Dinner with Friends (2001) masterfully explores the ripple effects of divorce through two married couples, adapting Donald Margulies' Pulitzer Prize-winning play with devastating intimacy. Director Norman Jewison brings the same careful attention to relationship dynamics he showed in Moonstruck (1987), letting the camera linger on uncomfortable silences and loaded glances. The film joins other powerful marriage dramas like Scenes from a Marriage (1973) and Kramer vs. Kramer (1979) in examining how divorce affects not just the separating couple, but their entire social circle.

sections.content: Dennis Quaid and Andie MacDowell deliver nuanced performances as Gabe and Karen, the seemingly stable couple forced to examine their own marriage when their best friends Tom (Greg Kinnear) and Beth (Toni Collette) split up. The film excels in small moments - like the contrast between a warm flashback dinner scene and its tense present-day echo. This technique recalls similar relationship autopsies in Blue Valentine (2010) and Revolutionary Road (2008).

What sets Dinner with Friends apart is its focus on the collateral damage of divorce - how it forces friends to take sides, reveals hidden fractures in seemingly solid relationships, and makes everyone question their own choices. The film shares DNA with Friends with Kids (2011) and Your Friends & Neighbors (1998) in examining how adult friendships weather major life changes. SUBHEAD: The Evolution of Marriage in Cinema

sections.content: Dinner with Friends arrived at a crucial moment in relationship cinema, bridging the gap between the bitter divorce dramas of the 1970s like An Unmarried Woman (1978) and the more nuanced explorations of marriage in films like Before Midnight (2013). Its honest portrayal of middle-aged disillusionment influenced later works like It's Complicated (2009) and Enough Said (2013).
